text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear, all you peoples—meaning all the tribes; and also, Give ear, O earth and all that fills it—the entire earth, for from there the evil spread throughout the earth. And let Hashem be a witness against you—Hashem is the One warning you. Hashem warns you from His holy sanctuary, while He is still in His sanctuary, before He goes forth from His place to judge the earth.
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: For behold—at the time when Hashem goes forth from His place (this expression signifies that He Himself will go forth to inflict punishment through His Providence, striking not through an emissary but in person, as in, “About midnight I will go forth into the midst of Egypt”).
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: And He will descend and tread upon the high places of the earth—using corporeal imagery, he depicts Him as first standing upon the lofty mountains.
text.0_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And they will melt—then the mountains will melt from dread of Hashem and the splendor of His majesty. The clauses correspond: the mountains will melt beneath Him like wax before fire, melting as readily as wax; and the valleys will split open like water poured down a slope—thus solid substances will become soft and fluid. This is a metaphor for the devastation of the land, which will become water again, as it was in the time of primordial chaos. (All this is figurative language, like “The mountains flowed before Hashem,” “The earth shook and quaked,” and similar expressions.)
text.0_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: For the transgression—all this will be for the transgression of Jacob—these are the ten tribes, who transgressed and deliberately rebelled against Hashem, worshiping idols and sun pillars. And for the sin of the house of Israel—these are the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, who did not rebel but sinned out of desire or error, as when they offered sacrifices at the high places. Although this was a sin, it was not rebellion, since most of these offerings were intended for Heaven. He explains: Who caused the transgression of Jacob, whereby the tribes worshiped idols? Was it not Samaria? For the monarchy in Samaria made the calves and enticed the people into this worship. And who caused the high places of Judah? Was it not Jerusalem? For the monarchy of Judah, situated in Jerusalem, brought this about by failing to abolish the high places until the days of Hezekiah.
text.0_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will make—this refers back to “And let Hashem be a witness against you,” for Hashem warns them, saying: I Myself will make Samaria a heap of ruins in the field, as its houses will fall and be destroyed. Afterward, I will make it a place for planting vineyards, and then I will pour its stones into the valley, for those planting vineyards will clear away the stones and remove the heaps left by the fallen houses, until I will lay bare even its foundations, as they will remove even the foundation stones to make the ground suitable for planting vineyards.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And all her carved images—the carved images were made of wood or stone, and people gave them hire and gifts; beneath them stood the idols. When the carved images are smashed, the idols will remain desolate. For she gathered it from a harlot’s hire—Samaria gathered all her wealth in this way, for she believed that all her prosperity came through idol worship, as it says, (Hosea 2:14) “Of which she said: These are my hire, which my lovers have given me.” Therefore, to a harlot’s hire they shall return—the king of Assyria will take them, as though his idols were giving them to him as hire. That is to say: I do not grieve at all over Samaria and its destruction, since they worshiped carved images and idols and strayed after others, forsaking Me.
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: (8–9) For this—but for this I will lament and wail, until I walk about like a madman, like someone who goes naked in his madness, because her wounds are grievous—a dangerous, contagious sickness that spread from Samaria to the land of Judah. They too suffered blows, although they did not worship idols in the days of Jotham and Uzziah, and their merchandise and hire were holy to Hashem. It seems more likely, however, that “her wounds are grievous” refers to the wounds Samaria inflicted upon Judah. He speaks here of the severe blows the ten tribes dealt Judah in the days of Ahaz, when Pekah son of Remaliah killed 120,000 in Judah in a single day. At that time, the Philistines also raided the cities of Judah’s lowlands and southern region, capturing several cities and settling in them (II Chronicles 28). (For in the days of Uzziah and Jotham there was peace in Judah. It is likewise difficult to interpret this as referring to Sennacherib’s invasion in the days of Hezekiah, since he would then have mentioned their deliverance as well.) He means that the wounds Samaria inflicted upon Judah were grievous and dangerous, for it has reached Judah—when Ephraim, Aram, Edom, and the Philistines invaded Judah—and reached as far as Jerusalem; but Jerusalem itself they could not conquer, as stated in Isaiah (chapter 7).
text.0_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Tell it not in Gath—after saying that he would lament like jackals, he now says that they should remain silent and not cry out, lest word be told in Gath. For Uzziah had taken Gath of the Philistines from them (II Chronicles 26), and it was under Judah’s control, while the Philistines were waiting to recapture it. Therefore, weep not at all, lest the Philistines learn of it and gain strength against you. Only in Beth-leaphrah, which belonged to Benjamin’s inheritance (Joshua 18:23), there roll yourself in the dust, for it is far from the Philistines, and your mourning and lamentation will not become known to them.
text.0_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Pass over. When the enemy came to the city named Shaphir, he stripped all its inhabitants naked but left them alive, because they did not fight him. The city of Zaanan, however, shut its gates and fought the enemy. Although the enemy killed everyone living in the houses surrounding the city outside its walls, they refused to open their gates. Therefore, when they were conquered, the enemy killed them all, rather than contenting himself with their spoil. Accordingly, he says figuratively, Pass over—shameful nakedness—to you, inhabitants of Shaphir. “Shameful nakedness” means the exposure of the private parts. He personifies nakedness and shameful exposure as an abstract entity: You, shameful nakedness, shall not go to Zaanan, for everyone there will be killed; instead, pass over to the inhabitants of Shaphir. For you, inhabitants of Shaphir, will go naked, with your buttocks exposed, and it is to you that I have commanded shameful nakedness to pass, for among you it will find people naked and shamefully exposed. But the inhabitants of Zaanan did not come out from within the walls, even to the mourning of Beth-haezel. Although all the neighboring houses raised a great lament over their dead, the people of Zaanan nevertheless refused to come out and open the city gates. Therefore, it will take its standing place from you—the lamentation will take its place among you, for there will be great slaughter in your city. In the city square they will hold the gathering where the mourner stands to lament those killed in the city and in Beth-haezel—that is, in the houses beside the city.
text.0_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: For she yearned. He explains why the inhabitants of Zaanan did not come out and upon whom they relied. For the inhabitants of Maroth—meaning Zaanan, which rebelled and refused to surrender to the enemy—hoped for good, expecting troops to come from Jerusalem to help them. Therefore, they rebelled and did not open their gates. He now explains why lamentation took its place among them and they were not delivered: For evil came down from Hashem to the gate of Jerusalem—through Hashem’s Providence, calamity descended upon Jerusalem, and they could not send troops to help the people of Zaanan.
text.0_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Harness the chariot to the swift steed, O inhabitant of Lachish. Idolatry first took root in Lachish. Thus we find that Amaziah king of Judah, who began worshiping the gods of Seir and whose servants rebelled against him, fled to Lachish and reigned there for twelve years, while Uzziah reigned in Jerusalem (as I explained in II Kings, chapter 14). Evidently, the priests of Hashem in Jerusalem opposed his idolatry zealously, whereas the people of Lachish supported him, and he reigned there for twelve years until the inhabitants of Jerusalem prevailed and killed him. There it says, “They carried him on the horses, and he was buried in Jerusalem.” The statement that they carried him on the horses means the following: Idol worshipers, whose principal worship was directed toward the sun, which they regarded as the queen of heaven, dedicated horses and a chariot to its worship. At sunrise, they would ride eastward to meet it with a chariot and horses, corresponding to their depiction of the sun’s journey along its circuit, as is known from ancient histories. Thus it says, (II Kings 23:11) “He abolished the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun, and burned the chariots of the sun with fire.” Amaziah had horses in Lachish dedicated to sun worship. Therefore, when the servants of Hashem prevailed and killed him, they carried his corpse upon the horses of the sun as an act of disgrace and contempt. It was their custom to make the sun’s chariots from broom wood, which retains the heat of a fire for many days (as our Sages stated in the chapter HaSefinah), symbolizing the sun’s heat and its enduring fire, for sun worship involved fire, as is known. Accordingly, he says, Cover the chariot with broom wood—cover the familiar chariot, the chariot of the sun, with broom wood. But to the swift steed—do not harness it to the horses dedicated to the sun; instead, harness it to a swift steed, fleet-footed for escape, so that they may flee from the enemy. Concerning this he says, She was the beginning of sin for the daughter of Zion—this was the first place belonging to the daughter of Zion, meaning the kingdom of Judah, where they began committing this sin of sun worship.
text.0_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: For in you were found the transgressions of Israel—sun worship, one of the transgressions of Israel, meaning the ten tribes, was found in you, even though you belong to Judah.
text.0_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore you shall give farewell gifts for Moresheth-gath. Gath had originally belonged to Israel from the days of David, who took Metheg-ammah from the Philistines, meaning the city of Gath (II Samuel 8:1). Rehoboam built it into a fortified city (II Chronicles 11), but afterward the Philistines took it from Israel. Uzziah king of Judah then conquered it from the Philistines and breached its walls (II Chronicles 26:6). In Rehoboam’s days, he also fortified Mareshah near Gath (II Chronicles 11:8). Once Gath’s wall had been breached, Mareshah protected Gath against recapture by the Philistines. It was called Moresheth-gath because it served as Gath’s defense. When the Philistines raided the cities of the lowlands in the days of Ahaz and sought to conquer Moresheth-gath so that they could take Gath, Pekah son of Remaliah was also waging war against Judah. The people of Lachish then reached an agreement with him to give him the city of Achzib, which was near Mareshah (as stated in Joshua 15:44), so that they could retain Mareshah, which protected Gath, and prevent Gath from falling into Philistine hands. Thus he says, Therefore you shall give gifts—meaning that you will give a present for, and on behalf of, Moresheth-gath. You will give as gifts the houses of Achzib to a deceiver—that is, to a deceitful man. He then explains who the deceiver is: to the kings of Israel. You gave the houses of Achzib as a present to the kings of Israel, who are false to their word, in order to save Moresheth-gath.
text.0_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Yet. This means: But you gained nothing by this, for the kings of Israel proved deceitful and did not keep their promise; they themselves took Mareshah from you. Whereas at first only the Philistines sought to possess Mareshah, now I will bring yet another heir to you, O inhabitant of Mareshah, for the kings of Israel also came to possess Mareshah. Moreover, they were not content to take Mareshah alone, for he shall come as far as Adullam—the second heir would reach Adullam, which was also a fortified city in that region and is listed among the fortified cities Rehoboam built. Pekah then took both Mareshah and Adullam from them. He explains: Who is this heir who will come as far as Adullam? The glory of Israel! That is, the army of the king of Israel and his splendor.
text.0_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Make yourself bald. Therefore, make your head bald and shear your hair, for your cherished children, for they have gone into exile from you. He adds, Make your baldness wide like the eagle’s, for birds of prey suffer from a disease that causes their feathers to fall out, especially the eagle, until eventually it loses all its feathers and dies from this. It may also be interpreted as follows: First, make yourself bald and shear your hair for your pampered children while they are still with you, for indulgence leads you to sin against Hashem. Afterward, make your baldness wider, for they have gone into exile from you.
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Woe to those who devise iniquity and work evil. While they are upon their beds, secluded by themselves, they cannot actually oppress or rob anyone, but can only devise iniquitous schemes. Yet upon their beds they devise iniquity—plans to oppress and rob—and also work evil. He explains how they can be regarded as working evil at that time: At the light of morning they immediately carry it out, because it is within the power of their hand. Thus, their devising of iniquity is considered as though they had already committed it, since nothing prevents them from putting their plans into action.
text.1_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And they covet. When they covet another person’s field, they seize it by force. Afterward, they covet houses; but since a house is situated in a city and cannot be openly seized, they take them through a business transaction, exchanging the fields they stole for the houses. Then they oppress a man and his house: after the exchange, they withhold the house from him—this is called oppression, for they retain what is rightfully due to him—which they can easily do even in the city. They also take a man and his inheritance: after seizing his fields, they ultimately take the owner of the field as well, for in his poverty he sells himself to them as a slave.
text.1_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, behold, I am devising against this family—these robbers—an evil that will be like an iron yoke around their necks, from which they will be unable to remove their necks. Nor will you walk upright, lifting your necks above the yoke, for it will be an evil time. When calamity comes upon individuals during a time of peace, there is hope that they may escape it; but when it is a time of calamity for the entire world, there is no possibility of escaping the evil.
text.1_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: On that day, one shall take up a parable against you and lament with a lamentation. He portrays the words that will be spoken concerning these plunderers as both a proverbial discourse and a lament. In a lament, one person chants the dirge and another responds; accordingly, he depicts one person as taking up the lament while the others answer him.
text.1_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: He shall say, “We have been utterly plundered.” He depicts figuratively how the enemies destroyed their houses and afterward divided their fields by lot. He portrays the aforementioned family, whose practice was to seize fields and exchange them for houses, as seeing the enemy plunder its house and saying, “We have been utterly plundered”—they have plundered my house. The respondent answers him—and this constitutes the lament—“He exchanges the portion of my people”: You acquired this house in exchange for the field, and now the enemy will make another exchange, returning the portion to its rightful owners. He then asks, “How does he remove it from me?” That is, how can he remove from me what belongs to me—namely, the field? Was not the field given to me in exchange for the house? The respondent answers, “To restore what was plundered, he apportions our fields”: The enemy apportions the fields in order to restore what you seized and plundered, since this is being done to take the stolen property from your possession.
text.1_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, you will have no one to cast a measuring line by lot. You will receive no portion in the redistribution of the fields, since the fields in your possession were stolen and are now being returned to their owners. This is a figurative way of saying that the enemy will destroy the houses but leave some of the poorest people of the land in the fields as vinedressers and farmers, so that they will regain the fields that had been stolen from them. But the family that seized fields and houses and enriched itself through robbery will have no portion or inheritance among the congregation of Hashem.
text.1_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not preach. He begins to dispute with them over their refusal to listen to the true prophets. The sense of the verse is: Is it said, O house of Jacob, “Do not preach what they preach”? This was a common saying among the house of Jacob: They would tell the prophets, Do not preach the things that they preach—do not utter prophecies of rebuke or predictions of calamity, which the prophets customarily proclaim and prophesy, for we do not wish to hear such prophecies. Secondly, they say, They shall not preach to these; disgrace shall not depart. The sense is: They shall not proclaim a disgrace that will not depart. At the very least, they should not preach rebukes concerning sins, thereby publicizing the people’s disgrace and evil deeds, for these humiliations and reproaches will never recede; rather, they will remain forever as a source of shame, as in, “His reproach shall not be blotted out.” They should not utter prophecies that will subject the people to everlasting humiliation.
text.1_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Is it said, O house of Jacob. All this is a saying spoken in the house of Jacob—that is, an expression commonly found upon their lips.
text.1_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: Is the spirit of Hashem constrained? They further argue against the prophets’ words foretelling punishment and calamity: Is the spirit of Hashem impatient? Does Hashem become emotionally affected by the evil deeds of human beings, His patience too short to endure them, so that in His impatience He becomes angry and wrathful and decrees calamity upon the people? Or, Are these His deeds? If you say that this is not because He becomes emotionally aroused to anger against those who transgress His will, as though He cannot remain patient, they ask: Are these truly His deeds—to inflict evil upon His creatures? Surely the deeds of Hashem are goodness, kindness, mercy, and grace, not the decreeing of evil and calamity. All this the house of Jacob says to the prophets. He answers them: Do not My words benefit one who walks uprightly? Why do you complain that My words are evil and announce calamity? For one who walks along the upright path, My words bring good and are not evil; rather, he rejoices in them, and they are words of consolation to him. The words of prophecy testify that Hashem watches over human conduct and repays each person according to his deeds. One who walks uprightly rejoices in this, for it allows him to hope in Hashem for righteousness and kindness in accordance with his conduct, as in, “It is a joy to the righteous when justice is done.”
text.1_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And against. If so, why do My words rise up against My people as an adversary and an enemy? Since My words benefit one who walks uprightly, how can those same beneficial words confront My people as an oppressive enemy? The reason is because of the garment: My words rise up against the garment and the cloak that you strip from those passing by securely. You strip peaceful travelers of their garments and the cloaks they wear, so that they resemble those returning from battle; for you attack wayfarers, wage war against them, and plunder their possessions as victors plunder those defeated in battle. It is against these evil deeds that My words rise up as an enemy.
text.1_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: You drive the women of My people from their cherished homes. As he will explain afterward, they would take women from their husbands’ homes as security for debts and defile them through fornication. Concerning this he says, From their children you take away My glory, for the children of these women became subject to doubts concerning their legitimacy, and the Divine splendor departed from them, since the Divine Presence rests only upon the families of Israel whose lineage is unblemished. He says to them: Will this continue forever? Will you drive the women of My people away forever, while I remain patient and silent toward you?
text.1_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Arise and depart from the land into exile, for this is not the resting place. You cannot rest in the land while conducting yourselves in this manner, nor can such a condition be called rest. He explains what he meant by “You drive the women of My people from their cherished homes.” He says, Because of defilement you take a pledge—you seize and hold a married woman as security, removing her from her husband’s home, in order to defile her through fornication. And with a grievous pledge—the pledge is explicit: you take her as security on the expressly stated condition that she submit to you and thereby be defiled. All this answers their demand that the prophets not prophesy rebukes and predictions of calamity against them. They had argued that it was inconceivable for Hashem to bring evil and punishment, asking whether Hashem was too impatient to endure their sin. In response, he shows them that Hashem cannot permit them to persist in their evil, for it violates all moral order. They have utterly corrupted their ways, so He is compelled to send them from the land, for this is not the resting place. He now returns to their saying, “Do not preach what they preach,” and says to them:
text.1_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: (11–12) If a man walking after wind—if I were to send you one of the false prophets, who would preach lies to you or speak according to the spirit of his erring imagination, telling you to indulge in wine and strong drink, he would be the preacher for this people: “I will surely gather all of you, O Jacob,” etc. This false prophet would proclaim in My name that I would gather Jacob and assemble them from the places of their dispersion—promises of good and consolation. He would prophesy to you that the assembled people of Jacob and Israel I would place together like sheep in Bozrah. That is, they would no longer bear the yoke of Torah and commandments, like sacred sheep, the sheep of Jerusalem, but would resemble the sheep in Bozrah, the capital of the kingdom of Edom. The “sheep” within it—meaning its people—are free from every Torah and commandment. He would tell you that you, too, would become like the nations, without Torah. If a prophet came and preached this to you, then like a flock within its fold, they would resound with the multitude of people. They would no longer hide in their houses as they did when fleeing from the true prophet who exhorted them to observe the commandments. Instead, they would all gather to hear his words, and the house of the preaching prophet would be filled with the clamor of people. Just as the fold where the sheep are gathered contains the entire flock, without a single sheep missing, so they would all be assembled there together, making a great commotion because of the multitude.
text.1_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: The breaker went up. He says: Observe how imperfect their faith is, how they sway like a reed before the wind and waver between two opinions. This was evident at that time in the tribe of Judah. Whenever a king arose who breached the boundaries of religion and practiced idolatry, the entire people immediately followed him and imitated his deeds, as occurred in the days of Ahaz and Manasseh. But when a righteous king succeeded him—such as Hezekiah after Ahaz and Josiah after Manasseh—and began to serve Hashem, the people likewise followed and all served Hashem. This demonstrates that faith was not firmly rooted in their hearts; rather, they followed whoever led them, whether toward Hashem or toward Azazel. Thus, when the breaker went up before them—the king who breached the boundary, violated the religion, and demolished its walls—then they broke through and passed on: they too breached the boundaries of religion, transgressed the laws, and violated the statute. They also broke through the gate and went out through it. At first, they breached the boundaries like thieves slipping through a gap; afterward, that breach became for them a permanent gate through which they passed, until they departed from the religion entirely. But when their king passed before them—when a righteous king led them, ruling in fear of Hashem and worthy to reign upon the throne of David—then Hashem was at their head: they followed Hashem and walked after Him.
text.2_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And I said. He further answers their claim, “Is the spirit of Hashem constrained? Are these His deeds?” He calls upon the leaders of the house of Jacob to judge the matter themselves and determine whether they do not deserve to be punished by Hashem according to justice. Thus he says, Is it not for you to know justice?—that punishment is rightfully due to them according to justice and law.
text.2_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Who hate. Since they hate good and love evil, which is the opposite of justice—as it says, “Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the gate” (Amos 5:15)—they strip the skin from the poor, and afterward strip their flesh as well from their bones.
text.2_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And those who. After they have already devoured the flesh of My people and stripped off their skin, leaving them nothing more to steal because they have plundered everything they possessed, then they break their bones, opening them to search for marrow. They also cut them apart and break the bones in two, as meat is placed in a small pot and the bones are broken, and like flesh within a cauldron, where the bones are boiled until all their marrow is extracted. In the same way, they oppress the poor in their possessions and their bodies until their very souls are crushed.
text.2_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Then. Since they commit such evil deeds, if then, at the time of calamity, they cry out to Hashem and He does not answer them, and He hides His face from them at that time, withdrawing His Providence and abandoning them to chance, is this injustice on His part? Surely, justice requires it, because they have made their deeds evil. How, then, can you ask, “Are these His deeds?” In accordance with the evil of their own deeds, He hides His face from them, and calamity comes upon them of itself, as determined by their conduct and the condition they have brought upon themselves.
text.2_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus says Hashem. Because they refused to listen to the true prophets and instead heeded false teachers and lying prophets, Hashem speaks concerning those prophets who lead My people astray from the proper path and prophesy solely for their own benefit. If they have something to bite with their teeth—if people give them food and thereby stop their mouths from speaking evil—then they proclaim peace. But against anyone who does not put food into their mouths to silence them, they consecrate war and prophesy evil, like the incident involving Bar Hedya in the chapter Ha-Ro’eh.
text.2_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, night shall come upon you because of vision. There were three types among them: visionaries, diviners, and prophets. Concerning the visionaries, since visions ordinarily come at night, he says that vision will no longer come through the night; rather, night will come upon you because of the vision. Concerning the diviners, since divination is ordinarily performed in a dark place, divination will no longer come through darkness; rather, it shall grow dark for you because of divination. Concerning the false prophets, who prophesied during the day, the sun shall set upon the prophets. He adds that not only will the sun set, but the day itself shall grow dark over them: while it is still daytime and the sun remains in the heavens, the day will darken over them. This means that calamity will overtake them before its appointed time.
text.2_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And they shall be ashamed. Consequently, the seers shall be ashamed, and the diviners shall be humiliated—humiliation being more severe than shame. The prophets who speak with their lips shall cover their upper lips, like a mourner who covers his mouth and refrains from speaking. The reason for all this is because there is no answer from God: none of their visions, divinations, or prophecies came in response from God; they were merely lies and the deceit of their own hearts.
text.2_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: But as for me, I am not like these false prophets. They have no answer from God in their mouths, but I am filled with power by the spirit of Hashem, Who speaks through me—not with false divination or a vain vision. They consecrate war against anyone who does not put food into their mouths, but I am filled with justice, to speak according to law and truth, and with might, so that I fear no man. They lead My people astray, but I am filled with strength to declare to Jacob his transgression.
text.2_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear this, please. After saying (in verse 1), “Hear, please, O heads of the house of Jacob,” and vindicating the ways of Hashem by showing that everything comes according to law and justice, he concludes his words: If so, hear this—what I now say to you. For you abhor justice, meaning established civil law, and also pervert everything upright—things required by reason—acting contrary to uprightness and reason. Thus, they obey neither the established laws accepted by society nor the dictates of sound reason.
text.2_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: (10–11) Who builds. That is, I ask them: Do they imagine that Hashem builds Zion with bloodshed, and that this is why, although its leaders judge for bribes, they rely upon Hashem, saying, “Is not Hashem in our midst?” Could they possibly think that Hashem loves bloodshed and injustice, and that with these He builds Zion and Jerusalem, so that even while judging for bribes they may rely upon Hashem, supposing that He desires such conduct and that through it Zion will be built and Jerusalem established? Surely Hashem builds Zion through justice and righteousness. Therefore, since its leaders, who are appointed to administer justice between one person and another, judge for bribes; its priests, who are appointed to issue religious rulings, teach for a price—declaring impure or pure, forbidden or permitted, according to the payment they receive—and its prophets do not prophesy but rather practice divination for money given to them, how can they rely upon Hashem, saying, “Is not Hashem in our midst?” How can they expect Him to protect them so that no calamity will come upon them?
text.2_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore. You will see the opposite: Because of you, Zion shall be plowed like a field. Zion will not be built through bloodshed; rather, it will be destroyed. He depicts the devastation as increasing with the degree of sanctity: Zion will be plowed until it becomes like a field; Jerusalem will not be plowed, but will become heaps of ruins through the collapse of its houses; and the Temple Mount, where the Temple and the altar stood and of which the Western Wall remained, will resemble the high places found in a forest, which no person enters, but where only foxes and wild beasts roam.
text.3_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be in the latter days. That is, now, because of you, “Zion shall be plowed like a field,” and this condition will continue until the end of days. Then, in the latter days, it will be rebuilt because we will walk in the name of Hashem our God and cast aside our evil deeds, as he concludes: “For all the peoples,” etc., “but we will walk in the name of Hashem.” Isaiah had already seen this prophecy (there, chapter 2), with slightly different wording, for no two prophets prophesy in precisely the same style. We have already explained it there in detail. He says that the mountain upon which the Temple will stand shall be firmly established at the head of the mountains and elevated still higher by the hills beneath it. Nevertheless, peoples will stream toward it like a river flowing toward a low place.
text.3_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And they shall go. Many nations will go and say to one another: “You go, and we will ascend with you to the mountain of Hashem; and from the mountain we will proceed to the Temple. He will teach us of His great ways, and we will then walk on our own in His particular paths.” That is, after He shows us the fundamental principles and foundations of the true religion, we will endeavor to understand its branches and details as well. For out of Zion, where the Sanhedrin and the teachers of religion will sit, the Torah shall go forth to the entire world; and the word of Hashem, meaning the word of prophecy, shall go forth from Jerusalem, for prophets will be found throughout the city.
text.3_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And he shall judge. The judge who will be there—the Messiah—will judge among many peoples. This means that the causes for which nation fights against nation and kingdom against kingdom will then cease. Sometimes war arises from differences in religion and belief; at that time, however, a universal Torah will go forth from Zion for them all. Sometimes war arises from disputes between one people and another, in which case the sword decides their quarrels; at that time, the Messiah will judge among many peoples. And sometimes rebellion arises within a country itself; concerning this he says that the Messiah will rebuke the nations and restore them to upright conduct through his reproof. Consequently, they shall beat their swords into plowshares, nation shall not lift up sword against nation, and they shall no longer study the strategies of warfare at all.
text.3_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And they shall dwell. Neither will strife and contention arise from a lack of food or from poverty, which causes people to turn to raiding and plunder, for every man shall sit beneath his own vine. And none shall make them afraid—shield, sword, and war will exist no more, forever.
text.3_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: For. He explains how Israel will merit all this glory in the latter days: Throughout the long period of exile, although all the peoples walk, each in the name of its god, nevertheless we will walk in the name of Hashem our God and will not forget the name of our God, although for His sake we are killed all day long. This will continue forever—that is, for a very long time—and therefore, in the latter days, the Torah will go forth from Zion to the entire world.
text.3_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: On that day, says Hashem, I will gather her who limps. I have already explained, regarding the verse “He shall gather the outcasts of Israel and assemble the dispersed of Judah” (Isaiah 11:12), that Israel—the ten tribes—was not widely scattered among the nations. Rather, they were driven from their place, cast into a distant land, and their location was lost. They therefore require gathering from the outside inward; concerning them He says, “I will gather her who limps.” The tribe of Judah, however, was scattered to the four corners of the heavens and therefore requires assembling; concerning it He says, “I will assemble her who was driven away.” The tribe of Judah suffers many evils and afflictions in the lands of its dispersion, unlike the ten tribes. Concerning Judah He says, And her whom I have afflicted—meaning the tribe of Judah, whom I afflicted, whether during the Second Temple period through the Greeks and afterward through the Romans, or throughout the duration of their exile.
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will make her who limps into a remnant. The ten tribes, whom He calls “her who limps,” were lost from the community of Israel and appear no longer to exist at all, or not to have remained faithful to their religion but to have become like all the nations. I will make them a remnant of Israel, and they will be revealed.
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: And her who was cast far away. This refers to the tribe of Judah, which remained the remnant of Israel but was driven farther and farther away, from nation to nation and from place to place. They became exceedingly weak and diminished through killings and upheavals, but I will make them into a mighty nation. And Hashem shall reign over them: 1] They will be under Hashem’s kingship and Providence. 2] His reign will be on Mount Zion. 3] It will endure from now and forever—from the time of redemption for all eternity, for they will never again be exiled.
text.3_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And you, O Tower of the Flock. He turns to the aforementioned Mount Zion and says to it: You, Mount Zion, are the tower of this flock—the flock consisting of those who limp and those who were driven away. At first you will be like a tower for sheep, and afterward you will become the stronghold, a mighty fortress. He explains that this will occur in three stages. First, the daughter of Zion shall come to you: the exiles will begin to assemble, and the exiles of Judah and Benjamin—the daughter of Zion, who were exiled from Zion at the destruction of the Second Temple—will gather to you. Afterward, the former dominion shall come: a limited government will arise among them, giving them a measure of authority and leadership, as Israel possessed in ancient times before any king reigned over the children of Israel, when judges led them. Finally, the kingdom shall come to the daughter of Jerusalem: they will possess an established monarchy, the kingdom of the house of David, when the Messiah afterward reigns over a firmly established kingdom. (This is likewise explained in Ezekiel 34:23–24 and 36:24–25, and Amos 9:11.) The kingdom of the house of David will be revealed gradually. At first, he will occupy only the position of a judge, and he will rise little by little until the kingdom belongs to Hashem, as explained there.
text.3_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Now. After revealing what will occur in the latter days, he returns to the intervening period, concerning which he said, “Therefore, because of you, Zion shall be plowed like a field.” In his prophecy, he sees what would occur in the days of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, culminating in the exile to Babylonia. He says, Now—meaning before the latter days—why do you cry aloud? Why do you raise the sound of a cry of destruction? Is there no king within you? Has your counselor perished? Surely, you still have a king and counselors. Why, then, have pangs seized you like a woman in labor? When a woman is ready for her womb to open and the child within her to emerge, labor pains and contractions seize her. This symbolizes her readiness for the gates of her city to be opened, for its inhabitants to go into exile, and for much blood to be shed within it. That is, how can you be ready to be conquered and led into exile while you still have a king and counselors? Why do you not gird yourselves with strength?
text.3_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Writhe. He answers: Indeed, you shall writhe; you shall also lie upon your belly and labor to bring forth the child, like a woman in childbirth. For now you shall go forth from the city—just as the child emerges from the womb, so shall you go forth from the city. And you shall dwell in the field, for many will settle in the open country, like those who went to live in Egypt and among the other nations surrounding the Land of Israel. And you shall come as far as Babylon—this refers to those who were exiled to Babylon. There you shall be delivered from the hand of your enemies, for those who dwelt in the field were afterward killed by the Chaldeans, as explained in Jeremiah; only the Babylonian exiles were spared. Likewise, there Hashem shall redeem you from the hand of your enemies, for the Babylonian exiles were redeemed and returned to the Land of Israel in the days of Cyrus.
text.3_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And now. He again turns back and sees in his prophecy what will occur after their redemption in the days of Cyrus. After they returned during the Second Temple period, many nations assembled against you—referring to the many different nations that subsequently gathered against Israel in generation after generation, such as the Greeks, followed by the Romans, and afterward throughout the long duration of the exile, until the final gathering against them in the days of Gog and Magog. His words encompass all of this, for he sees many nations repeatedly assembling against Israel after their redemption in the days of Cyrus.
text.3_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: Who say, “Let her be defiled, and let our eyes gaze upon Zion.” This means that these gatherings will take two forms. At times, they will want Zion to flatter them—that is, to be humbled and subjected to them, like a servant who flatters his master. This occurred in the days of the Greeks and Romans, who wanted Israel to be subject to them and pay tribute. At other times, they will say, “Let our eyes gaze upon Zion.” That is, they will believe that the visions the prophets saw concerning Zion were spoken about them—that they have taken Israel’s place, that Hashem will dwell among them, and that the seers’ visions concerned them. The Ishmaelites think this, and for this reason they will assemble an army against Jerusalem to conquer it, as is known, and others will do likewise. For the same reason, the armies of Gog and Magog will gather to conquer Jerusalem and behold there the visions seen by the seers, which, in their opinion, were prophesied about them.
text.3_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: But they do not know the thoughts of Hashem. Hashem’s counsel is the intended purpose of His action, whereas His thoughts are the means He employs to prepare for that counsel, which is the ultimate purpose. The prophet explains that every gathering of the nations against Zion forms part of Hashem’s thoughts—that is, these gatherings serve as means through which His counsel, His intended purpose, will be accomplished. All their gatherings will be preparations and means leading to the gathering in the latter days, which itself will be a preparation through which He will accomplish His counsel. There He will judge them for their deeds, and there they will recognize the true religion. Through the signs and wonders they witness at that time, the survivors will return to the true faith, while the wicked will perish like chaff swept from the threshing floor. Thus he says, They do not know the thoughts of Hashem, nor do they understand His counsel—that all these things are means through which His counsel will be accomplished, namely, that He has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor. Just as sheaves are gathered to the threshing floor to be threshed, so that the chaff and husk may be removed and the pure grain left behind, so will He thresh them in the war of Gog and Magog. He will remove the chaff—the wicked who acted evilly against the holy—and refine the grain, from among whom righteous converts and those who recognize the true religion will emerge.
text.3_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion. He depicts the time of the war of Gog and Magog, when He will gather them like sheaves to the threshing floor in order to separate the chaff from the grain. He commands the daughter of Zion to arise and thresh like a threshing heifer, for I will make your horn iron, enabling you to fight with your horn and gore the multitude of Gog, and I will make your hooves bronze, for the work of threshing and separating the grain from the chaff. And you shall crush many peoples, removing the husk—that is, destroying the wicked—until only pure flour remains. And I will consecrate their ill-gotten gain to Hashem: the profit and plunder they took from Israel will become devoted property, sacred to Hashem, for Israel is holy to Hashem, and their property is therefore like consecrated property. And their wealth—even their own wealth, which was not gained by plundering Israel and is therefore not devoted property—will nevertheless belong to Hashem, because He is the Master of all the earth, and everything belongs to Him.
text.3_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Now. He explains who the nations are that will assemble against Jerusalem at that time and whom Israel will thresh. He says that the host that will come against Jerusalem in the latter days will consist of the descendants of the nations that besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in ancient times, such as the descendants of Assyria, Babylonia, and Rome. Thus he says, Now gather yourself in troops: the troop that will assemble at the time of the war of Gog will be the daughter of the troop that laid siege against us in ancient times. Those descended from the host that besieged us in former days will now assemble in the army of Gog and Magog. Likewise, they will be the descendants of the host that struck the judge of Israel upon the cheek with a rod, whose ancestors struck Israel’s judges upon the cheek with a rod. (A blow upon the cheek is an act of humiliation, as is a blow with a rod; how much more so when one is struck upon the cheek with a rod. They did this to the judge of Israel, and certainly to the common people.) The descendants of that host will gather against Jerusalem and receive their retribution in the latter days.
text.4_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: But you, Bethlehem. It has already been explained in Ezekiel, chapter 37, that at the time of the end, the ten tribes will first awaken, with the Messiah son of Joseph as their king, and they will achieve great strength. The tribe of Judah, scattered among the nations, weak and few in number, will join them and remain subordinate to them under the rule of the Messiah son of Joseph. Afterward, the Messiah son of David will arise through the might of Hashem, and they will all accept the kingdom of the house of David. Wars will then cease, for nations will seek him, and his resting place will be glorious. Our visionary prophet explains these matters to us, saying: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, from which David, son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, emerged and the kingdom of the house of David arose, are too young to be among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for Me one who is to rule Israel. That is, at present you are still too young and insignificant, even together with the thousands of Judah who accompany you, to attain the stature required for the man designated for Me to come forth from you and rule Israel. You are still too small and weak, even with the thousands of Judah beside you, to prevail in this manner—until you exercise great dominion and the Messiah who emerges from you, the Messiah son of David, gains the strength to rule Israel, whose origins are from ancient times, from days of old. That is, he will attain a powerful kingdom corresponding to his ancient origins in the days of David and Solomon, who ruled a great and mighty kingdom. For this, you are still too young, weak, and lacking in strength, even together with the thousands of Judah who are with you.
text.4_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore. The sense of the verse is: Therefore, until the time when she who is in labor has given birth, and until the time when the rest of his brothers return, He will place them over the house of Israel. Therefore, throughout the period before the ingathering of the exiles is complete—which is compared to a woman giving birth, as it says, “For Zion has both labored and given birth to her children”—and until the rest of Judah’s brothers return to their land, He will place them—the thousands of Judah—under the authority of the house of Israel. That is, as long as the general ingathering has not been completed and all the exiles of Judah have not yet assembled in the Land of Israel, the house of Israel—the ten tribes and the Messiah son of Joseph, who comes from among them—will remain predominant. They will be the warriors and rulers, while the house of Judah will be subordinate to them. (As stated there in Ezekiel: “Behold, I am taking the stick of Joseph,” etc., “and I will place them upon it, together with the stick of Judah,” as I explained there.)
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And he shall stand. But afterward, the Messiah from Bethlehem Ephrathah will arise—that is, he will stand firm and prevail over the nations—and shepherd Israel. He explains: He shall stand in the strength of Hashem, confronting the nations through Hashem’s power, and he shall shepherd in the majesty of the name of Hashem his God, tending Israel through the holiness of Hashem’s name, as it says, “He shall be imbued with the fear of Hashem, and he shall not judge by what his eyes see.” And they shall dwell. From that time onward, they will no longer wage war but will dwell in tranquil security, as it says, “His resting place shall be glorious.” For now, etc.
text.4_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: (4–5) And he shall be, etc. This means that he will now become great to the ends of the earth, and this will be achieved through peace. The greatness of the Messiah will extend to the ends of the earth, not through wars but through the power of peace. This itself will constitute his greatness: he will have no need for war, for all the peoples will accept his Torah, his religion, and his sovereignty over them. The sense of the verses is: And this shall be peace, and it shall deliver us from Assyria when he comes into our land. Peace will then save us from Assyria, so that we will not need to fight against him as in the past; for the peace prevailing at that time will save us from Assyria, since he will submit to us and seek a covenant of peace. The passage from Assyria, when he comes into our land, etc., through and the land of Nimrod at its entrances, is parenthetical. That is, until now, before the Messiah son of David arose, while the Messiah son of Joseph reigned, we required warfare throughout the wars of Gog and Magog. If Assyria came into our land during that period, or even when he trod within our borders, we had to raise against him seven shepherds to fight him. They shepherded the land of Assyria with the sword, for sword and warfare were necessary; and they also shepherded the land of Nimrod—the country of Babylonia, where Nimrod was the first king—at its entrances, for they had to advance as far as the entrance to their land and subdue and break them there through warfare and siege. But now it will no longer be so. Rather, this shall be peace, and it shall deliver—peace will deliver us from Assyria when he comes into our land. Regarding the seven shepherds and eight princes, the commentators have offered many interpretations. It may also be said that this alludes to the earlier period: From the time the enemy began to cut Israel down—which occurred in the days of Jehoahaz son of Jehu (II Kings 13:7)—until the king of Assyria came and exiled them in the days of Hoshea son of Elah, there were eight princes, meaning eight kings of the ten tribes: Jehoahaz; his son Joash; his son Jeroboam; his son Zechariah; Menahem; Pekahiah; Pekah; and Hoshea—eight in all. (Shallum was killed immediately and is therefore not included in the count.) Afterward there were seven shepherds from the house of Judah: Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah. It may also be interpreted as referring to the future. According to Ezekiel’s prophecies concerning the wars of Gog and Magog in chapters 32 and 38, the war prophesied in chapter 32—in which Assyria will come against the Land of Israel to wage war with Edom, as I explained there—will involve seven shepherds: Egypt, Elam, Meshech, Tubal, Edom, the princes of the north, and the Sidonians. The war prophesied in chapter 38 will involve eight princes: Gog, prince of the land of Magog; Meshech; Tubal; Persia; Cush; Put; Gomer; and the house of Togarmah. I explained there that on one occasion he will come into the land but will not enter Jerusalem; concerning this he says, “When he comes into our land.” On another occasion he will come as far as Jerusalem; concerning this he says, “When he treads within our palaces.”
text.4_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And the remnant of Jacob shall be. Even the remnant who remain at that time among the nations and do not go to the Land of Israel will be like dew from Hashem. That is, unlike the present, they will not receive their sustenance through the nations among whom they dwell, but will be like dew that comes directly from Hashem. They will also resemble showers upon the grass, which cause the grass to grow without receiving any benefit from it. Likewise, they will bestow goodness and kindness upon the nations among whom they dwell but will receive nothing from them, for they will not depend upon man to obtain goodness and kindness from him; rather, they will receive all their abundance directly from Hashem, without any intermediary.
text.4_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And the remnant of Jacob shall be. With regard to their strength against their oppressors—whereas until now Israel was like a scattered sheep among lions, as it says, “Israel is a scattered sheep; lions have driven him away”—they will now be like a lion and a young lion. There is a distinction between “nations” and “peoples”: nations are of lower standing than peoples and have no king, whereas peoples are distinguished and possess a king. Conversely, “nation” denotes a larger collective than “people.” The lion is mature, while the young lion is youthful. A lion customarily goes out into the forest in search of prey and tears apart large animals, whereas a young lion lies in ambush in its lair, does not go out in search of prey, and tears apart only small animals. He therefore depicts Israel as being among the nations—the larger but less distinguished collectives—like a lion among the beasts of the forest. Although the nations resemble large wild animals, Israel will be like a great lion in comparison with them, going out to the lands of the nations to wage war against them and seize prey among them. But among many peoples, which are smaller than nations but more distinguished, Israel will be like a young lion among flocks of sheep. Just as a young lion does not go out in search of prey, Israel will not go forth to fight them in their own lands, for most of them will accept the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven. Only those who come to Israel’s dwelling place to wage war against them in the Land of Israel—such as the peoples who will march against Mount Zion in the army of Gog and Magog—will be torn apart like prey seized by a young lion in its lair, while they will be as weak before Israel as flocks of sheep. He explains: Which, if it passes through, tramples—the mature lion passes through the forest outside its lair and tramples, whereas the young lion tears its prey within its lair, and none can deliver from their grasp.
text.4_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Your hand shall be raised. They will not need to fight their oppressors with both hands; it will suffice to raise a single hand over your adversaries. There is a distinction between an adversary and an enemy: an adversary actively oppresses and fights against someone, whereas an enemy seeks his harm but does not actively attack him. Against the adversaries who fight you, your hand will be raised, while all your enemies shall be cut off by themselves.
text.4_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be. This means that the situation described above will prevail at first, while the war of Gog is still being waged against them, when they will need to tear their enemies apart and raise their hand against them. But on that day—meaning after the war of Gog and Magog—they will no longer need warfare at all, for Hashem will cut off their enemies. Warfare requires: 1] Horses and chariots; concerning these He says, I will cut off your horses. 2] Cities containing weapons and fortified cities; concerning these He says:
text.4_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will cut off the cities of your land. This means the cities belonging to the land and the state, for the chariot cities and the cities containing weapons did not belong to the people as individuals, but to the state as a whole, and were therefore called “the cities of the land.” Concerning the fortresses, He says, And I will demolish all your strongholds. 3] They had sorcerers and soothsayers to determine when they would succeed in war; concerning this He says:
text.4_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: (11–13) And I will cut off sorceries from your hand. 4] They had among them the worship of carved images, sacred pillars, and Asherah trees. Concerning this He says, And I will cut off your carved images, etc., and I will uproot your Asherah trees and destroy your cities—meaning that the cities in which they practiced idolatry will be treated like cities condemned for idolatry.
text.4_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will execute. Then I will execute vengeance upon the nations that refuse to return to the true religion and accept upon themselves the kingdom of Heaven, as explained at the end of Zechariah.
text.5_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear now. After saying above (3:1), “Hear now, O heads of the house of Jacob,” because he wished to present his dispute with Israel before them so that they might serve as judges in the matter—as he said, “Is it not for you to know justice?”—they refused to listen. He therefore tells them that Hashem has chosen other judges in their place to hear His claim, dispute, and argument: the mountains and hills, before whom He will present His case. Hashem said to the prophet, Arise, contend before the mountains—that is, present Hashem’s case before them—and let the hills hear your voice. Although the leaders of the house of Jacob refuse to listen, the hills will hear the prophet’s voice.
text.5_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear, O mountains, and you enduring ones—that is, the mighty mountains, which are the foundations of the earth, existing since the time of Creation, when they served as the earth’s foundation as it emerged from the deep.
text.5_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: For Hashem has a dispute. He has a dispute with them because they sinned against Him, and with Israel He will argue, demonstrating that He is just in His dispute.
text.5_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: My people. He sets forth the argument He has with them: What harm have I done to you? On the contrary, remember the benefits I bestowed upon you. And how have I wearied you? In return for the good I did for you, you were obligated to show gratitude and serve Me. Did I weary you by demanding burdensome service in return for those benefits?
text.5_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: For I brought you up. He explains, “What have I done for you?” The first benefit was that I brought you up from the land of Egypt. Although this occurred before the appointed time, while you were still in the house of bondage, nevertheless I redeemed you before that time. And I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, through whose merit you were sustained, as our Sages said: The manna came through the merit of Moses, and so forth. They also taught you the proper path—Moses instructing the men, Miriam the women, and Aaron serving as Hashem’s priest.
text.5_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: (5–8) My people. He now explains, “How have I wearied you?” Remember, please, what Balak king of Moab devised—he wanted Balaam to denounce Israel and curse them—and what Balaam answered him: that it was good in the eyes of Hashem to bless Israel, because Divine Providence was attached to them for their benefit. Balaam therefore advised Balak to cause them to stumble through the daughters of Moab, so that Hashem’s Providence would depart from them. From this you can see that I did not weary you. As evidence, he cites what occurred at that time from Shittim to Gilgal. The proper sense and sequence of the verses is: From Shittim to Gilgal, in order that you may know the righteous acts of Hashem: He has told you, O man, what is good, etc. The two verses, “With what shall I approach Hashem?” etc., and “Will Hashem be pleased with thousands of rams?” etc., form a parenthetical statement, as will be explained. The meaning is that after Israel sinned at Shittim through Balaam’s counsel, they regretted their deeds and asked what would appease Hashem, atone for transgression, and bring sin to an end. They imagined that they would need to appease Him with enormous sacrifices, even offering their children and the fruit of their bodies to atone for their sins. Then, from Shittim to Gilgal, He told you, O man, answering their question by revealing what is good: Hashem does not desire burdensome forms of service, but only to practice justice, etc. That is, Moses then undertook to explain the Torah and wrote Deuteronomy for them, telling them what is good and what Hashem requires of them: He does not demand burdensome service, sacrifices, and offerings. Indeed, Deuteronomy does not elaborate upon the laws of the sacrifices. He desires only that they practice justice and kindness. This occurred from Shittim to Gilgal: At Shittim, Moses began explaining Deuteronomy to them; after Moses’ death, until their arrival at Gilgal, the miracle of the Jordan was performed for them and they saw that Hashem’s Divine Presence had returned to dwell among them. Hashem spoke to Joshua and commanded him to guard the Torah and observe its commandments, without burdening them with any difficult service, until they reached Gilgal, where He commanded them to circumcise themselves again and to offer the Passover sacrifice, which was a demanding service. But until they arrived at Gilgal, He required no such service from them. Thus he says, From Shittim to Gilgal, He told you, O man, what is good—that Hashem requires no burdensome service from you, but only that you practice justice, etc.—so that you may know the righteous acts of Hashem. Through this, you will recognize Hashem’s righteousness: He does not burden a person with difficult forms of service intended to weary him.
text.5_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: With what shall I approach Hashem? In a parenthetical passage, he relates what Israel said after they stumbled at Shittim through the worship of Baal Peor. They asked, With what shall I approach Hashem? With what offering or gift shall I come before Him, inasmuch as He is Hashem, Who brings all existence into being? They further asked, With what shall I bow before the God Most High? Since I have sinned before Him, I must bend myself low, submit, and seek forgiveness. With what shall I bow before Him, inasmuch as He is the God Most High? On account of His strict judgment, He is called “God,” and He is the God Most High; one who sins before Him therefore deserves severe punishment. Corresponding to their question, “With what shall I approach Hashem?” he explains: Shall I approach Him with burnt offerings, by bringing Him year-old calves as burnt offerings?
text.5_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Will Hashem be pleased? Surely He will not be pleased even with thousands of rams, which are superior to calves, or with tens of thousands of rivers of oil that I might bring for the libations accompanying the burnt offerings. He now explains their corresponding question, “With what shall I bow before the God Most High?” Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression? It would seem that for my transgression—deliberate rebellion—I should offer my firstborn son as a sacrifice; and for the sin of my soul—an inadvertent sin—I should offer the fruit of my body, meaning my younger children. This is what they asked at that time.
text.5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: He has told. This returns to the preceding passage: In response to your question, He told you, from Shittim to Gilgal, what is good and how you may find favor with Hashem. He has told means that He told you: 1] What is good for you insofar as you are a human being—the commandments governing relations between one person and another, which are beneficial to human beings themselves in civil society. He also told you what Hashem requires of you—the commandments governing the relationship between man and God. Corresponding to “He has told you, O man, what is good,” he says, only to practice justice and to love kindness. These are good for you insofar as you are human: justice protects civil society from robbery and oppression, while through acts of kindness one person assists another. Corresponding to “What does Hashem require of you?” he says, and to walk humbly with your God. You must walk with your God—as in, “Noah walked with God”—and this is the foundation of the commandments between man and God: to walk with God, follow His ways, and sanctify oneself with His holiness, as it says, “You shall be holy, for I am holy.” This must be done humbly and in private, for these are matters between you and your Creator. Modesty is proper here, so that a person does not act presumptuously or become prideful in investigating matters concerning Divinity, nor presume to be wiser than His commandments; rather, he should walk humbly with God.
text.5_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: The voice of Hashem. The sense of the verse is: The voice of Hashem and sound wisdom call to the city whose name is Yir’eh. He refers to the verse, “And Abraham called the name of that place ‘Hashem Will See.’” The city was originally called Shalem, as it says, “Melchizedek, king of Shalem,” and Abraham added the name Yir’eh, because Hashem would always see and exercise Providence over this city. The prophet now addresses Jerusalem, telling it to remember that its name is Yir’eh, for the eyes of Hashem are always upon it, and therefore it must guard itself against rebelling before His glorious eyes. Thus, the voice of Hashem, together with sound wisdom—meaning the Torah—called this city by the name Yir’eh, for Hashem approved this name and recorded it in His Torah. If so, hear the rod and Who has appointed it. Since Hashem watches over your deeds, heed the rod—the punishment appointed for your sins—and consider Who appointed that punishment: surely it is Hashem, Who possesses the power to punish. That is, your stubbornness may arise from one of three thoughts: You may think that Hashem does not see your deeds; against this he says, Your name is Yir’eh. You may think that He does not intend to punish; against this he says, Hear the rod. Or you may think that He lacks the power to punish; against this he says, Who has appointed it.
text.5_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Is there yet? Accordingly, he asks: Are there still treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked? Does he not fear the punishment of Hashem, Who sees his deeds? And an accursed ephah established by the rulers—even the ephah established by the officials appointed to supervise weights and measures and ensure that the ephah is an honest measure is accursed, for Hashem is enraged by it, since even the rulers enact statutes of iniquity.
text.5_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Shall I be innocent? Because they established a smaller ephah, they would also falsify the shekel: since the sellers reduced the ephah, the buyers would reduce the shekel. Nevertheless, they would not thereby be innocent, for concerning this it says, “Differing weights and differing measures—Hashem abhors them both.” This means that even when both are found together—when, because there are differing weights, the seller also uses differing measures, giving a reduced ephah to one who pays him with a small, falsified shekel—it nevertheless remains an abomination in the eyes of Hashem. The presence of both does not justify him in saying that he reduced the shekel because the other party reduced the ephah, or vice versa, for Hashem prohibited differing weights and differing measures under all circumstances. Thus he says: Shall I thereby be innocent with wicked scales and by having deceitful weights in the bag, reducing the shekel because the ephah was reduced, when Hashem abhors them both?
text.5_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Whose rich men are filled with violence. For they falsify both the measure of the ephah and the measure of the shekel, as it says, “Making the ephah small and the shekel great.” And its inhabitants speak falsehood, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth. Ordinary speech is an overt lie, while calculated speech, which is attributed to the tongue, is deceit: through it they deceive so artfully that the falsehood cannot be detected.
text.5_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, I too have begun to strike you with sickness. Consequently, I continued striking you with the rod, as it says, “Hear the rod and Who has appointed it,” until I made you sick. Since none of this proved effective, I must therefore make you desolate because of your sins, until you become utterly desolate.
text.5_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: You. He explains what is meant by “I have afflicted you by striking you”: Although you will eat but not be satisfied, nevertheless your food will bring you low within you—the food within you will make you sink down, an illness ordinarily caused by excessive satiety and overeating.
text.5_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: And you shall attempt to rescue. You will try to recover your property and produce and save them from the enemy’s hand, yet you shall not succeed in rescuing them from him. Moreover, because of what you do rescue from the enemy, I will deliver you to the sword—they will kill you with the sword on account of it.
text.5_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: You shall sow. A curse will likewise fall upon the produce of the ground and the fruit of the trees: You will sow grain and legumes but will not reap them; and although you tread olives, you will not anoint yourself with their oil, for the enemies will consume it.
text.5_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And they are observed. He now explains what He meant by “to make you desolate because of your sins.” Although I afflicted you by striking you, it accomplished nothing, for the statutes of Omri are still observed—he added evil statutes to the sins of Jeroboam—and likewise all the practices of the house of Ahab are observed, for they went still further in evil; and you walk according to their counsels. Therefore, I must make you desolate because of your sins. Thus He says, so that I may make you a desolation—utterly desolate—and you shall bear the reproach of My people. That is, you will bear punishment for the reproach of My people, which you caused by making them an object of disgrace through your evil deeds.
text.6_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Woe is me. The prophet laments the low state of the generation: all the pious and upright have vanished and disappeared from the land, and he alone remains faithful to God. He compares the generation before him to a vineyard of grapes or a grove of figs whose season has already passed. Among the figs, he is like one who gathers the summer fruit after the first-ripe figs have already been taken, while he alone remains like a fig left at the end of summer. Among the grapes, he is like the gleanings remaining after the vintage. Corresponding to the gleanings of the vintage, he says, There is no cluster to eat; and corresponding to the gathering of summer fruit, he says, There is no first-ripe fig to eat, which my soul desires. He longs to eat a cluster or a first-ripe fig, but there is none.
text.6_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Has perished. He explains the corresponding phrase, “There is no cluster to eat”: The pious man has perished from the land. The pious person does more than he is strictly obligated to do, both in the commandments between man and God and those between one person and another. He resembles a cluster filled with grapes, for he is filled with the fruits of righteousness and justice. Thus our Sages interpreted eshkol as “a man in whom everything is found.” Such a person has perished from the land. Corresponding to “the first-ripe fig that my soul desires,” he says, There is no upright person among men—not even a person who at least acts uprightly in matters between one person and another. Therefore, he says “among men,” referring to commandments governing relations between people. Even such a person does not exist. On the contrary, they all lie in wait for blood, seeking to shed blood, and each hunts his brother with a net, setting a snare and trap to capture him.
text.6_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Concerning the evil. The order of the verse is: Concerning the evil committed by the hands, the prince inquires and the judge investigates, in order to favor the evildoer in exchange for payment. That is, although you see the prince and the judge asking about the evil committed by someone’s hands—questioning, investigating, and examining the wrongdoing—do not think that they do so to administer justice and punish the evildoer. Rather, they investigate in order to favor him in exchange for payment. By paying them a bribe, the evildoer induces them to treat him favorably and refrain from punishing him. The prince was charged with disciplining wrongdoers, while the judge was charged with examining the case according to law; yet both the prince and the judge accepted payment and favored the evildoer. Above them stood the great man, the head of them all and the preeminent member of the Sanhedrin. When people could obtain no justice from the prince or the judge, they went to this great man. And the great man declares the ruin desired by his soul—in order to favor him in exchange for payment. The great man also desires a bribe. He therefore declares that this evil deed warrants the ruin of the evildoer’s soul—that he deserves death and that destruction and calamity should befall him—but he merely says this. Thus, the prince and judge investigate, while the great man declares that the evildoer deserves destruction; yet all of this is done only to favor him in exchange for payment. Both the investigation by the prince and judge and the great man’s declaration that the evil committed deserves ruin and destruction are merely intended to extract bribes from the offender, after which they will favor him. And they weave it together. The three—the prince, the judge, and the great man—then agree to favor the evildoer and form a threefold cord, for, as our Sages said, a cord consists of no fewer than three strands. That is, they issue a forceful and binding judgment, like a threefold cord that cannot be broken, firmly confirming that the evildoer deserves no punishment.
text.6_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: The best of them is like a thorn; the most upright is worse than a thorn hedge. Even the good person found among them is not inherently good. He resembles a thorn that appears straight in comparison with a thorn hedge. A thorn hedge is a fence or covering made from thorns and briars. The thorn itself is full of twists, but when it is fashioned into a hedge, it is bent still further and becomes even more tangled and twisted, so that by comparison the individual thorn appears straight. Likewise, even the best among them is crooked and perverse; he is considered upright only in comparison with the members of his generation, who are as twisted as a thorn hedge. The day of your watchmen—your visitation—has come. On the day of calamity prepared for those who watch you—that is, the nations waiting to behold your misfortune—on the very day appointed for their punishment, your own visitation has also come: your sins have been remembered, and you will be punished for them. Thus, on the day prepared for the punishment of the nations neighboring the Land of Israel, Israel too was called to account for its sins, so that now their confusion shall come. The entire people, of whom he said, “They all lie in wait for blood,” etc., will become bewildered, and confusion will prevail among them.
text.6_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not. This means that the confusion among them will be so great that their hearts will become divided, each person from his brother, until they will not trust even a friend whose affection they had previously trusted, nor place confidence in a guide—the leader who teaches them and directs their path. Even from her who lies in your embrace, guard the openings of your mouth, for peace within the home will also cease.
text.6_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For a son dishonors his father. Even one’s own offspring will rise against their parents, demonstrating the utmost confusion and corruption of the people. Every bond of love and kinship will be severed; all the more so will there be no civil peace among them.
text.6_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: But as for me. The prophet says: In view of the degradation of this generation, its corruption, and the evil state of its public and domestic life, there is no hope at present. But as for me, I will look to Hashem. Looking denotes expectation directed toward a distant time: I will look to Hashem’s promise that He will yet return and redeem us in the latter days. I will wait. That is, within this expectation of the future redemption in the latter days, there are two possibilities. One is to hope and wait until the arrival of the appointed time and the end of days, when the redemption must come under all circumstances. The term “waiting” applies to awaiting something certain to come, like waiting for morning, which will surely arrive when the night ends. Concerning this he says, I will wait for the God of my salvation—for the appointed time of salvation. Alternatively, the redemption may come even before its appointed time if they repent, seek His presence, and an acceptable time arrives, as it says, “In an acceptable time I answered you, and on a day of salvation I helped you” (Isaiah 49:8), as I explained there. Concerning this he says, My God will hear me—He will hear my prayer at an acceptable time, even before the time for which I wait.
text.6_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not. Therefore, do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I am in exile, for though I have fallen, I shall arise. Through my very fall into the depths of the pit, I will rise and regain strength, for through it I will be saved. Moreover, though I dwell in darkness—the darkness of affliction—Hashem is a light to me. Even if I lack physical light—the light of material prosperity—I possess the light of Hashem: the light of religion and faith, and the light of hope in Hashem’s salvation.
text.6_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Indignation.
