Through this fall, I will bear the indignation of Hashem, because I have sinned against Him, and thereby my sins will be cleansed and my iniquity atoned for, until He pleads my cause. At the time of redemption, He will plead my cause and execute judgment for me against those who oppress and afflict me. Then He will bring me forth into the light, and I will behold His righteousness. Until that time, the light arising from Hashem’s righteousness already exists, but I sit in darkness and my eyes are closed from perceiving Hashem’s righteous acts. Then He will bring me forth into the light, and I will behold Hashem’s righteousness, His light, and His salvation. Looking back, I will then understand the righteousness He showed me and recognize that everything was an act of righteousness and kindness for my benefit.
text.6_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And my enemy shall see. My enemy, too, will see this at that time, and then shame shall cover her, for throughout the exile she said to me, “Where is Hashem your God?”—why has He withdrawn His Providence from you? She will then see that Hashem was with me throughout all the days of my exile, that He never hid His face from me, and that everything occurred through His Providence so that He might benefit me in the latter days. But my eyes shall look upon her: when I lift my eyes to behold her, they will look upon her with contempt. Even now, although she now prospers and grows powerful, I see that she shall be trampled like mud in the streets. Her prosperity is itself preparing her downfall, so that she will ultimately perish and be trampled underfoot. This is what I see in her even now, during the days of her tranquility.
text.6_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: (11–12) A day. He turns toward the congregation of Israel, and the clauses correspond to one another: A day for rebuilding your fences—that day is firmly established; though the appointed time of that day is distant, it shall come to you. That is, the day prepared for rebuilding your fences—within which, like sheep gathered into newly built folds, the scattered flock will be assembled—that day is firmly established before Hashem. It also means that this day will truly be day, with no night accompanying it, whereas the days preceding it will be night rather than day. He then says again: Although the appointed time of that day is distant—its fixed time is indeed far off, in the latter days—nevertheless, it shall come to you, as it says, “Though it tarries, wait for it, for it will surely come.” From Assyria—it will come to the returning exiles from Assyria and the fortified cities, where they were exiled in the days of Sennacherib; and from the fortress—meaning the exile in the land of Egypt—as far as the River Euphrates, as it says, “Those lost in the land of Assyria and those driven away in the land of Egypt shall come,” and, “Hashem shall utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian Sea and wave His hand over the River.” And sea—those exiled toward the west, namely, the exiles caused by the Romans—shall come from the sea; while the exiles of the north shall come from Mount Hor, which lies north of the Land of Israel.
text.6_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And the earth shall be. Then the earth—meaning the entire globe—shall become desolate because of its inhabitants, for the iniquity of the earth’s inhabitants will be visited upon it. Thus he says, because of the fruit of their deeds.
text.6_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Shepherd Your people. When the seer perceived how long the exile would endure, he prayed that Hashem would have mercy upon them throughout that period. He says to Hashem, Shepherd Your people with Your staff. Even if You must strike them during the days of their exile, nevertheless shepherd Your people through Your Providence, as a shepherd tends his flock. Do not strike them with the staff of destroyers; rather, chastise them with Your staff—with the rod of men, not with a club or cudgel. The flock of Your inheritance, dwelling alone in a forest—shepherd them in the midst of Carmel. They dwell alone—that is, separated from all workers of iniquity—yet they remain in a forest filled with savage, predatory beasts. I therefore ask: Shepherd them in the midst of Carmel, a fruitful land filled with grain—that is, watch over them so that they possess everything they need—until the time comes when they shall graze in Bashan and Gilead as in days of old, meaning that they will return to the Land of Israel.
text.6_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: As in the days. This is Hashem’s answer: As in the days when you came forth from the land of Egypt, when they too were afflicted and oppressed and I brought them out with great power, signs, and wonders, so I will show them wonders in the future.
text.6_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: They shall see. The nations that see this with their own eyes shall be ashamed of all their might, for they will recognize that their strength is vanity and emptiness when Hashem performs wonders, and that no man prevails through strength. They shall place their hands over their mouths and utter nothing, for their lips will be unable to express these awesome wonders, which surpass human understanding. Their ears. That is, they will not place their hands over their ears, as at the Exodus from Egypt, concerning which it says, “The peoples heard and trembled,” for their ears shall become deaf. The meaning is that they will not merely hear reports with their ears; rather, they will see Hashem’s deeds and wonders with their own eyes.
text.6_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: They shall lick the dust like a serpent. He adds, like creatures that crawl upon the earth, for a serpent sometimes raises its head, whereas these nations will remain entirely prostrate. He further says, They shall tremble from within their enclosures. They will not be like a crawling creature able to creep wherever it wishes, for fear will confine them within their cities. This fear will arise not from warfare or widespread slaughter; rather, they shall be in awe of Hashem our God because of His greatness and exaltedness, and consequently they shall fear you, because Hashem is with you.
text.6_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Who is a God like You? In concluding his words, he gives thanks to God for the forgiveness of sins, for Hashem will bear the transgression of His people. He says: You are God—who is like You, bearing iniquity? Although You initially chastised them for their sins, nevertheless, for the remnant of His inheritance—the generation that will remain at the end of days—He bears iniquity and passes over transgression. Among the Thirteen Attributes it says, “Bearing iniquity, transgression, and sin.” “Bearing” means that He carries and tolerates the sin without punishing it, although it remains preserved before Him until the appropriate time, as indicated by the words, “Yet He will not entirely acquit.” In the future, however, there will be a difference: transgression, meaning rebellion that does not constitute iniquity—that is, rebellion not arising from heresy or a distortion of the intellect—He will remove entirely. Iniquity, however, He will not remove from existence; it will remain as before, when He bore and tolerated it without removing it. The attribute of patience results from His bearing iniquity and transgression rather than removing them entirely: He tolerates them and postpones His anger instead of punishing immediately. In the future, when He removes transgression entirely, the attribute of patience will apply only to iniquity, which He will not remove but will continue to bear patiently. He therefore adds, He does not retain His anger forever. Even regarding iniquity, toward which He exercises patience and which remains preserved before Him, He will not retain His anger forever. This will result from the awakening of two other attributes: mercy and abundant kindness. Concerning this he says, for He delights in kindness, and will forgive out of kindness. And also:
text.6_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: He will again have mercy upon us and forgive through the attribute of mercy. Through these attributes, He will subdue our iniquities: He will no longer bear iniquity as a burden that He carries and tolerates, but will suppress it so that no punishment will ever result from it in the future. (You already know the dispute in which one Sage says that He “subdues” iniquity and another says that He “bears” it; the iniquity itself is not erased.) And You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea. Sin, however—an offense committed inadvertently or because of desire, rather than through rebellion or heresy—You will cast into the depths of the sea, so that it will no longer exist at all.
text.6_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: You will grant. After enumerating all the attributes, he turns to the attribute of truth and the attribute of preserving kindness for thousands of generations. He says that the attribute of truth means that You will fulfill Your promise: You will grant the truth—the promise You made to Jacob, when You told him, “Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread out westward and eastward.” This means that after the exile, when their souls cling to the dust, He will arise to help them, and they will spread through an inheritance without boundaries. You will fulfill this promise through Your attribute of truth. You will also grant the kindness that You promised to Abraham. In Abraham’s case, God had not yet become obligated by any previous promise, and therefore it is called “kindness.” In Jacob’s case, however, He was already obligated to fulfill the oath He had sworn to Abraham and Isaac, and therefore it is called “truth.” Thus, You will preserve what You swore to our forefathers; although the oath dates from days of old, You preserve kindness for thousands of generations.
